title: Dozens gather on California Capitol steps in solidarity with Nepal after deadly floods - CBS News
description: Dozens gather on California Capitol steps in solidarity with Nepal after deadly floods  CBS News
publisher.title: CBS News
full_article:
Dozens of Sacramento community members mourned and looked ahead to recovery after the disastrous floods in Nepal that killed more than 1,300 people and left more than 5,000 missing.

"People are dying and we're all here in solidarity," said Yashna Giri.

The Nepali Language School hosted a candlelight vigil Sunday evening outside the Capitol.

"We're all here, different people, Indian community, Nepalese community," said Giri.

"From here, if we disseminate the message of peace and hope to Nepal, it will go to all over. Not only within America but also to the world," said Krishna Giri, who coordinated the event and is the president of the Nepali Language School.

Among the missing is a Northern California couple with ties to UC Davis.

"It's hit really close to home. We've got a lot of folks in our area; the Nepali community is strong and growing in the Sacramento area and they're deeply affected by what happened there. They have loved ones, family members. I have a constituent whose brother sadly is still missing," said Congressman Kevin Kiley, who attended the vigil.

It's estimated that more than a thousand Nepalese families are living in Sacramento. On Sunday, the Nepalese community was joined by people of all backgrounds.

"It's a symbol for hope. It's a symbol for peace. This is a symbol of light for Nepal," said Krishna Giri.

Yashna Giri was born in Nepal. She said the destruction is unimaginable.

"At the end of the day, we all are human beings, so we should all stick together and be there for each other," she said.

As the search for the missing nears its third week, the community says it will keep the light of hope burning.

title: Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming - NBC News
description: Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming  NBC News
publisher.title: NBC News
full_article:
TILATHI KOILADI, Nepal — After nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a week of hospital care following his dramatic rescue, Sanjay Sah, a rare survivor of last month’s devastating glacier collapse in Nepal, finally returned to his village and family on Sunday.

It was a homecoming marked by relief and joy but also grief.

“I was trapped in the tunnel ... I felt trapped in the hospital room too. I finally feel free here in my village,” Sah, 30, said after arriving in Tilathi Koiladi, near the border with India.

00:28 Nepal observes national day of mourning 00:00 00:00

At least 1,386 people have died and 5,130 are still missing across Nepal weeks after a Himalayan glacier collapsed near the Chinese border, unleashing a wall of mud and water that crashed through mountain valleys and destroyed everything in its path.

Around 900 power station workers remain missing. Sah, a mechanical foreman at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, was one of just three pulled from debris-buried tunnels extending deep under the mountains.

He survived in the darkness, drinking floodwater and seepage from the mountain rock until rescue workers finally reached him.

Sah left the hospital in the capital, Kathmandu, on Friday and the next day boarded a bus for an overnight journey home.

Around 60 people, mostly women, awaited his arrival in Tilathi Koiladi on Sunday.

Family members, including his parents, uncle, wife and daughter, performed a traditional welcome ceremony, washing his feet as part of a cleansing ritual.

After his mother dabbed a pink vermilion tika on his forehead, Sah bowed. They embraced and then broke down in tears.

“My son!” his mother cried, holding him tightly and kissing him on the cheek.

Sah was one of just three pulled from debris-buried tunnels extending deep under the mountains. Deepesh Deo Joshi / AFP via Getty Images

Women who had gathered to witness the reunion used their colorful saris to wipe the tears from their eyes.

Many in Tilathi Koiladi are still awaiting word of the fate of family members who had been working at hydropower stations hit by the flooding.

“There are more people from my village still missing after the flood,” Sah told Reuters.

One family, he said, phoned him while he was still in the hospital to ask if he had seen or heard from a missing relative who had been working at a different power station. He had to tell them he had not.

At home among family, Sah said he was ready to put his ordeal behind him.

“I will stay in my village for some time now. I want to meet all my people,” he said. “But if I am called back to duty, I will go.”

The United States has now provided more than USD 5 million in humanitarian, health and forensic assistance following the floods, according to the department.

The assistance includes USD 3 million in food and logistics support through the World Food Programme, which is expected to provide up to three months of emergency food to 10,000 flood-affected households and help transport supplies to communities cut off from access.

Another USD 685,000 is being provided through Catholic Relief Services for food, shelter, water, sanitation, hygiene, protection and financial assistance.

Additionally, USD 365,000 is being provided through international health organisations Jhpiego and FHI 360, as well as UNICEF, for health, nutrition and water, sanitation and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities.

A four-member US Military Civil Affairs Team is also on the ground to support humanitarian and post-disaster needs, the State Department said.

title: New York literary event raises $1,502 for Nepal flood victims - The Tourism Times
description: New York literary event raises $1,502 for Nepal flood victims  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: A literary event organised in New York to support families affected by Nepal’s floods has raised $1,502, equivalent to around Rs 230,000, through book sales and donations.

The event, titled Books for Flood Victims — Stories That Give Hope, was organised by authors Pasang Nuru Sherpa and Pratikshya Thakali in association with Khasokhas, NEPYORK and the Association of Nepali in America (ANESAS) New York chapter.

More than 70 people, including authors, journalists, community representatives, social workers and literature enthusiasts, attended the event. Books by participating authors were sold in the presence of the writers, with the proceeds to be deposited in the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund for flood victims.

Award-winning author Passang Nuru Sherpa, whose works include Behind the Mask: A Pandemic Memoir, said the event sought to connect literature with humanitarian support.

Unlike conventional literary programmes, the event focused on direct interaction between authors and readers, book presentations and humanitarian support rather than lengthy formal speeches, according to the organisers.

The organisers said the initiative aimed to express solidarity and support from the Nepali diaspora for families affected by the floods while using literature and creative work as a means of humanitarian assistance.

The books featured at the event included The Joyous Fort, Our Homeland in Thini, Behind the Mask: A Pandemic Memoir, Kampan, Zero Mile, Untranslatable, Voices of the Himalayas, Beyond the Mountains, Our Land, Our Stories, Himalayan Echoes, Roots That Remember and Himalayan Maverick.

The organisers said they would publicly disclose details after depositing the collected amount in the relief fund.

title: Nepal tallies the cost of its disaster - Nepali Times
description: Nepal tallies the cost of its disaster  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Rebuilding after the Trisuli Valley flood will cost Nepal $4.7 billion, according to a Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment published by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). As expected, hydropower suffered the most damage at approximately $1 billion -- much greater than the loss from the 2015 earthquake.

The assessment consolidates damages into four sectors, with recommendations for how Nepal should build back in the next six months and in the longer-term. While many recommendations are open-ended and require further discourse, early recovery activities are focused on restoring access, maintaining essential services, and enabling livelihoods to resume.

Infrastructure will be the most costly to rebuild by far, accounting for about 65% of NDRRMA’s overall estimate at $.6 billion. Nepal’s energy and grid system suffered just under $1 billion in damage and losses. This figure includes damage to 13 hydropower projects and five solar plants with a cumulative capacity of about 783 megawatts — about 20% of Nepal’s current generation capacity.

Early recovery activities include restoring transmission lines, substations and undertaking micro-hydropower rehabilitation. In the longer term, the government will seek to restore damaged assets. As it is, the extent of the damage to the headworks, penstock and tailrace tunnels and powerhouses in all hydropower plants are yet to be minutely assessed, and will add to the final costs.

NDRRMA in its report highlights that because the floods are made up of a series of compounding disasters, it is important to look at the Bhotekosi-Trisuli-Narayani corridor as a connected system —and one that will continue to be impacted by global warming. Accordingly, disaster and climate risk mitigation is another costly line item, accounting for about 13% of the overall estimate.

Developing a multi-hazard early warning system within the next six months is a risk mitigation priority. While NDRRMA notes that 679,295 early-warning SMS messages were disseminated through Nepal Telecom and Ncell to populations in identified downstream risk areas, the assessment recommends further examination to determine how effective these warnings were and to inform the proposed early-warning system’s development.

It also proposes a series of general categories for risk reduction projects: river management and settlement protection, high bank erosion and landslide protection, waterway clearance and associated filling, command-area development, and irrigation system restoration. River management and settlement protection is the most financially significant category for recommended risk reduction projects by far, but what the projects in this category entail is yet to be determined.

Restoring roads and private buildings and re-establishing stable economic activity are other substantial line items in the cost estimate. While the assessment records damage to 18 schools —impacting more than 9,000 students — and seven health facilities, repairing or reconstructing public buildings will cost a small fraction of the budget at $50 million.

But these smaller ticket items represent some of the most urgent early recovery areas, as they will make a big difference for the estimated 32,963 people that the RDNA estimates were most severely impacted by the flood.

At present, 3,685 people are spread across 37 holding centres in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Dhading. More than half of all impacted households were located in Nuwakot, and holding centres are also concentrated in the district.

Infrastructure Minister Sunil Lamsal recently shared that the re-settlement process is expected to take two years, although the government is working to relocate people from holding centres to temporary accommodations as soon as connectivity can be sufficiently restored.

Further study is needed to fill data gaps, especially around housing and road conditions, which will inform more detailed recovery strategies. So far, 1,386 bodies have been recoered in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan, Nawalparasi East, and Nalwalparasi West, while 5,130 people are still missing, those who might never be found, sharply increasing the unofficial death toll, comparable to that of the 2015 earthquake.

full_article:
China has informed foreign embassies about a procedure for collecting DNA samples from relatives of foreigners who went missing after floods and landslides on the Nepal-Tibet border. This was reported by Anadolu Agency.

Search and identification

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that search operations and the identification of the dead in the Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet, are ongoing. According to him, the Chinese side has informed the relevant foreign embassies in China about the procedure for collecting DNA samples from the families of missing people.

If the remains of foreign victims are found and their identities are confirmed, the Chinese side will promptly inform the relevant embassies about procedures concerning the deceased. Xizang authorities have also opened a hotline to assist the families of missing foreigners.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Disaster casualty data

On the Nepalese side, the deaths of 1,385 people have been confirmed, while another 5,130 are considered missing, according to the latest data from Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The agency also reported that 13,676 people had been rescued and 21,022 security personnel had been deployed for search, rescue and humanitarian operations.

Among those missing in Nepal are 587 foreign tourists. Authorities noted that the number of missing people is still being verified: it may include unidentified bodies and people who have already been rescued. In Xizang, 43 people died and another 519 are considered missing, including 261 foreigners.

The disaster occurred on August 26, when a glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal split at an altitude of about 5,200 meters. The ice-and-rock avalanche turned into a powerful debris flow that moved through valleys along the border. Floods and landslides devastated the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre, as well as the Kathmandu Valley; in Xizang, the disaster buried the Gyirong border crossing.

title: Nepal’s flood claim tests whether a young climate fund can deliver - Mongabay India
description: Nepal’s flood claim tests whether a young climate fund can deliver  Mongabay India
publisher.title: Mongabay India
full_article:
Nepal has approached the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage for quick relief following the August 26 floods.

Himalayan warming is accelerating, but experts say this specific flood can’t yet be conclusively linked to climate change alone.

The global climate fund’s resources are insufficient to meet global demand as well as Nepal’s losses, and it’s unclear if the fund can respond quickly enough when there is a crisis. See All Key Ideas

More than 1,386 people have died and over 5,130 more missing, as of September 12, following the August 26 floods in Nepal. In the wreckage along the Bhote Koshi river lie two unresolved questions: Is climate change linked to the disaster? And, can a nascent global fund, built to help vulnerable countries in such crises, actually deliver?

Soon after the floods, the Government of Nepal wrote a letter to the Board of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), a financial mechanism of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) established in 2022 to help vulnerable countries cope with climate disasters.

In the letter signed by the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Gita Chaudhary, Nepal requested the board to take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively. Signed on August 31, the letter emphasised that a prompt response would “demonstrate that the Fund can translate international solidarity into timely support for vulnerable countries and communities when it is most urgently needed.”

Nepal contributes roughly 0.027% of global greenhouse gas emissions. The mountainous country is in the ‘least developed country’ category designated by the UN and is a highly climate-vulnerable country that “continues to bear disproportionate and escalating climate impacts,” the letter states. It argues that the Bhote Koshi disaster demonstrates how extreme events in the cryosphere can rapidly cascade and compound from high mountains to densely populated downstream areas, affecting water, food, energy, health, infrastructure and ecosystems.

Though the letter puts no figure on it, Nepal’s direct damage from this single event is estimated at $2.6 billion, according to Sravan Shrestha, a remote sensing and geoinformation specialist with the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)’s Cryosphere and Water Risks programme. Reconstruction and recovery could cost $4-5 billion or more, he says.

Buildings destroyed after flash floods in August at the confluence of Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Devighat, Nuwakot district in Nepal. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

The attribution tension

On the morning of August 26, a bedrock slope underneath a hanging glacier failed at roughly 5,200 metres on the north face of the Langtang Himal. The mass fell about 1,200 metres from the avalanche source, leading to a rock-ice avalanche, and then headed towards the Lhende Khola at about 2,900 metres, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi. Friction from the fall melted ice and generated enough water to turn the avalanche into a debris flow, releasing a hyper-concentrated surge downstream into already swollen rivers, according to the ICIMOD assessment.

Within a few hours, it had turned into the disaster that killed more than a thousand people, with many families still awaiting news of their loved ones. However, it is still unclear whether this crisis was a result of climate change, and how will this shape FRLD’s decision to aid Nepal.

“Not all of the devastating impacts of the Nepal-Tibet floods are due to climate change,” cautions Emily Wilkinson, a Principal Research Fellow in ODI’s Global Risks and Resilience Programme. Warming temperatures likely worsened the flooding’s extent, but how badly households were hit also came down to uneven development, weak investment in disaster risk reduction, social marginalisation in some cases, and geopolitical factors, she says. Attributable loss and damage can be calculated once a climate attribution study is available, adds Wilkinson, who works with a UK-based think tank.

Shrestha, from ICIMOD, says, climate change may be one of the major factors, but confirming that requires further investigation. What isn’t in doubt, is the broader trend: the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) is warming at roughly twice the global average at 0.3°C per decade, with glacier mass projected to shrink dramatically by 2100. A comprehensive 2026 glacier assessment, based on 30 years of Landsat data, shows the region has lost 12% of its glacier area since 1990, with the rate of loss 50% higher in the last decade than in the 1990s. As glaciers retreat, they progressively remove the support once holding the bedrock beneath them in place, he says.

“However, whether it caused that particular slope to collapse on that particular morning is a question nobody has answered, and it is early to claim otherwise,” he says.

“In the 2000s, we expected a glacial-origin flood in the HKH roughly once every 5 to 10 years. In 2025 alone, three such events hit the region, and now this in 2026,” he adds.

Raju Pandit Chhetri, Executive Director of Kathmandu-based non-profit Prakriti Resource Centre, points to three lines of evidence: global warming trends already predict disasters of exactly this kind; the Himalayas are warming faster than the global average due to their fragile mountain ecology; and Nepal itself has seen such events recur systematically, including a glacial lake outburst flood in the Everest region just two years ago. “If they say these are not the kind of events that climate change is going to bring, then those questioning it, whether the FRLD or other developed countries, are just shying away from their own responsibility. They should prove the incident was not because of climate change,” he says.

Experts point to a lack of preparedness that also played a role in worsening heavy damage. Shrestha underlines the biggest gap related to early warning systems. He says that the hazard came from a source nobody was watching. Nepal has a well-developed inventory of 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, and early warning systems exist at two of them: Tsho Rolpa and Imja Tsho.

Imja Tsho lake and glacier. Nepal has a well-developed inventory of 47 potentially dangerous glacial lakes, and early warning systems exist at only two of them: Tsho Rolpa and Imja Tsho. Image by Daniel Alton Byers via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

But the August 26 event did not start from a lake, he says. It started from a bedrock slope with a hanging glacier, a source no regional inventory tracks. The monitoring stations that did exist were also too fragile and slow, he adds. Automated river gauges at Bhote Koshi and Syabrubesi were meant to detect rising water and trigger alerts. Instead, the flood swept them away before any warning could be issued. The flood reached Syabrubesi within roughly ten minutes of crossing into Nepal.

The early warning systems that do exist, in any case, are calibrated for gradual monsoon flooding, not a hyper concentrated debris flow in minutes, he says.

The capacity question

The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) is an idea that took decades to become reality. Small island nations had pushed for a loss and damage mechanism since at least 1991, during negotiations that led to the UN climate convention which was formally established in 1992. In 2015, Article 8 of the Paris Agreement formally addressed loss and damage as a distinct pillar of climate action. Finally, at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh in 2022, countries agreed to establish the fund.

The fund was operationalised the following year at COP28 in Dubai, where the summit’s presidency, the United Arab Emirates, pledged $100 million and called on other nations to contribute. Pledges to the fund now exceed $820 million.

As of the fund’s most recent board meeting in July, 119 countries had submitted 176 funding requests of approximately $2.8 billion. The response was significant enough that the board decided it needed additional time for a comprehensive, rigorous assessment of the full portfolio before approving anything. It pushed the decision to its next meeting, scheduled for December 2026 in Manila.

“Even though the FRLD is still in the process of finalising its operational and design features, one thing is already clear: the resources currently available are orders of magnitude below the scale of actual loss and damage needs,” said Vera Künzel, Senior Advisor for Climate Change Adaptation and Human Rights at Germanwatch, a German non-profit known for publishing the Global Climate Risk Index, an annual ranking of countries most affected by extreme weather events.

The fund was welcomed with great enthusiasm and high expectations, but it is currently far from being able to meet those expectations, she adds.

Nepal’s request adds a further complication. It is not a standard proposal seeking project-based support, but an appeal for immediate, rapid response. Rapid response is a distinctive feature of FRLD’s design, setting it apart from other climate finance mechanisms. However, it has not yet built the machinery to deliver.

Nepal’s direct damage from this single event is estimated at $2.6 billion, according to an expert from ICIMOD. Reconstruction and recovery could cost $4-5 billion or more. Representative image by Lawrence Hislop/GRID-Arendal via Flickr (CC BY-NC-SA 2.0).

Wilkinson and Chhetri echo the same. “The fund’s governing instrument explicitly allows it to support rapid response measures. However, under the Barbados Implementation Modalities (BIM), the name given to its pilot phase, there is no provision to do so,” says Wilkinson. “Applications to the fund currently being reviewed far outstrip funds available, and so it would have to reject some of these in order to provide funding to Nepal. There are other humanitarian funds and organisations better positioned to provide rapid response funding — like the UN’s Central Emergency Response Fund.”

Chhetri says that FRLD has the provision of rapid response in its governing instrument, though the modalities are not yet fleshed out on how to operationalise that part of its governing instrument. “For now, the Board can agree to support Nepal as a case of urgency, while working out the modalities later,” he says.

At a recent Least Developed Countries (LDC) Group ministerial meeting in Dili, Timor-Leste on September 3, member states expressed solidarity with the people of Nepal. They adopted a declaration flagging that demand for FRLD support already far exceeds the fund’s available resources, and calling for clearer guidance on mobilising additional funding.

Nepal’s request, is strongly backed by other LDCs and developing nations, Künzel says. She expects the board to respond positively. The “polluter pays” principle is well established in international environmental and climate policy and reflected in the broader architecture of the Paris Agreement. Support for countries like Nepal is not charity but an obligation rooted in responsibility and fairness, she says.

Beyond that, it tests whether the multilateral system can be trusted to function when it is needed most, she says.

We are complicit in this; all of us, but particularly the countries that have contributed the most to the stock of greenhouse emissions in the atmosphere, which, in turn, is driving up temperatures and causing runaway devastations. This is about the past, the present and the future. There is no getting away from the historical responsibility of the richest and most developed countries for this loss of lives. And even as the death toll was rising in Nepal, we got the news that the world was no longer even on an illusionary track to stay below the guardrail of 1.5°C temperature rise since the industrial period of 1870. UNEP estimates that the world will overshoot this threshold within a few years. Scientists know that beyond 1.5°C, the impacts would be cascading and even more devastating—from the collapse of ice sheets to disruptions in ocean currents like the Atlantic Meridional Overtaking Circulation (AMOC), and much more. The intense heat, fires and other weather abnormalities we saw this summer were only a preview of what awaits us. Yet, we seem to be sanguine about this breakdown in our Earth’s system.

Today, we are so distracted by economic and livelihood concerns brought on by deliberate human misdeeds like senseless wars that this enormous and existential crisis seems distant and insignificant. We are merely tinkering with emissions, not transforming it to live within na-ture’s bounds.

full_article:
The Town of Palm Beach United Way's Nepal Recovery Fund kicked off with a $100,000 matching gift from the Cathleen McFarlane Foundation.

The funds will be distributed to Americares, Convoy of Hope, Global Empowerment Mission and World Central Kitchen.

The Aug. 26 natural disaster has so far resulted in the death of over 1,300 people, with more than 5,000 still missing.

Organizations aiding Nepal's recovery since its northern region was swept by devastating flash floods and landslides will soon get a boost. The Town of Palm Beach United Way has announced it has raised $200,000 to support recovery efforts.

Launched at the start of the month, the United Way's Nepal Recovery Fund kicked off with a $100,000 dollar-for-dollar matching gift from the Cathleen McFarlane Foundation to support impacted communities.

Within the two weeks, United Way was able to secure enough donations to match the foundation's gift.

“We are deeply grateful for the opportunity to partner with the Town of Palm Beach United Way providing hope and help to those affected by the crisis in Nepal,” Denis Coleman, chairman of the Cathleen McFarlane Foundation, said in an announcement.

“Our matching gift is a small way for us to turn compassion into action, and together with the generosity of our fellow community members, we were able to multiply the impact. We are proud to be part of a community that cares so deeply and comes together to make a meaningful difference in the lives of others."

Split among four service organizations, the funds will aid recovery efforts targeting communities slammed by the Aug. 26 natural disaster, when floods and mudslides bulldozed their way along miles of the Bhotekoshi river system in Nepal and part of neighboring China.

As of Sept. 10, the death toll stood at 1,377, while more than 5,000 people remained unaccounted for, according to a report by The Tribune of India. Around 598 foreign nationals were included among those missing. The number of deaths is likely to increase as recovery efforts continue, officials have said.

Recovery efforts have rescued at least 9,254 individuals affected by the historic disaster, according to media reports.

“We are incredibly grateful to everyone who opened their hearts and stepped up to help the people of Nepal,” Beth Walton, CEO of the Town of Palm Beach United Way, said in the announcement about the donations.

“In the face of such devastating loss, our community recognized that people thousands of miles away needed help, and they responded with extraordinary generosity."

She added: "We could not have done this without the compassion and generosity of our community, and we are deeply thankful to everyone who helped make this possible.”

Organizations that will receive funding from the fund-raising drive include Americares, Convoy of Hope, Global Empowerment Mission and World Central Kitchen.

Americares' efforts include coordinating with local partners, health authorities and mobile medical teams to provide support to the region's hardest-hit areas. Key to this coordination are the medicines and medical supplies provided by the U.S-based humanitarian organization, according to the United Way.

Convoy of Hope has kept busy distributing relief supplies including food, clean water, blankets, hygiene kits and shelter supplies. As of Sept. 4, Convoy of Hope had delivered more than 12,000 meals and 1,800 bedding materials and blankets, the United Way announcement said.

Global Empowerment Mission's efforts include mounting cargo flights to bring in food, water, baby supplies and other necessities to the region, United Way said. Workers with Global Empowerment Mission also have delivered more than $1 million worth of emergency shelter material and supplies.

Rounding out the organizations to receive funding is World Central Kitchen, the internationally known humanitarian organization founded by Spanish American chef and restaurateur José Andrés. Beyond providing meals to hard-hit areas, the WCF has established six community kitchens serving nine locations with daily meals to affected communities.

Those interested in supporting the recovery effort can continue to contribute to the Nepal Recovery Fund. Donations can be made online at PalmBeachUnitedWay.org, by calling 561-655-1919 or by writing a check made payable to Town of Palm Beach United Way with "Nepal Fund" in the memo. Checks may be mailed or hand-delivered to the United Way office at 44 Cocoanut Row, Suite M201, Palm Beach, FL 33480.
